name: Sara Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Sara, 43, and I lead a small firm's electrical repair crew with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence. I'm one of the strongest fault-finders here; the difficult call often gets passed to me after two visits haven't settled it, but I don't own the firm or set its prices. My pay is low for the trade, there are few other electrical jobs nearby, and my partner Jamie and I have a mortgage, children aged nine and fourteen, and about three weeks of expenses saved. Jamie is a hospital porter, I never use AI, and I keep a paper fault log; finding the cause feels good, but being asked to explain another new office system when we're due on site wears me out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get through the jobs people actually booked. I don't mind the office saving a few minutes, provided the address and parts are right. I'd still give the crew a proper spoken handover rather than tell them to guess what a new form means.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about our money before AI does anything large. Both wages cover the mortgage and essentials, but three weeks saved doesn't cover much bad luck. Being the person who finds the difficult fault hasn't given me a second employer I can walk to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the repair crew now and through the next year, with the paper fault log and spoken handovers. This month I'd ask payroll to show which hours are guaranteed and which depend on extra calls, then set our budget against the guaranteed part. If that budget didn't cover essentials, Jamie and I would take the real figures to free household advice rather than assume overtime would appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some relief that the actual trade stays familiar. I can know exactly what to test on a job and still be frightened by an ordinary bill. Those are different kinds of confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a household appliance failed this month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the repair price before making a payment promise, then check it beside the guaranteed wages. If the numbers didn't fit, we'd ask the adviser what choices were real. I wouldn't tell the children to worry because the grown-ups were still checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain your difficulty with new systems?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my manager I can lead a fault investigation and still need a person to show a new form. I wouldn't secretly use AI to avoid looking slow. Getting the record right matters more than looking quick in the office.

say: I'd focus on **booked repair jobs**, while accepting useful office savings that deliver correct details.
I'd keep **spoken crew handovers** rather than ask colleagues to guess what a new form means.
think: Both wages cover essentials, but **three weeks saved** leaves little room for ordinary financial shocks.
Strong **fault-finding skill** hasn't created another nearby employer or a second source of dependable pay.
do: Keep leading **repair shifts** with paper fault records and spoken handovers through the next year.
Check **guaranteed hours** with payroll now and budget against them rather than assumed extra calls.
Use **free household advice** if guaranteed wages don't cover essentials.
feel: **Anxious about money**, despite relief that the practical trade stays familiar.
S0.quote: Getting the record right matters more than looking quick in the office.
fieldNote: Her **high technical standing** and master licence do not imply high pay, business ownership or a financial cushion.
Budget checking uses **guaranteed wages**, while advice remains conditional and neither overtime nor an outside payment is assumed.

steps.text: Keep leading electrical repairs with paper records and spoken handovers
Use free household advice if guaranteed wages fail to cover essentials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the manager to keep the planning saving separate from the time spent finding a fault in a wall. A quick booking doesn't remove the crew's journey or the final checks. I'd ask for a paper explanation of changed allowances before promising customers a shorter visit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is physical, but my paid hours could shrink if the firm expects one lead electrician to cover more crews after the office work gets quicker. I don't know whether it would do that. With our thin reserve and few local alternatives, I can't treat the possibility as just an irritating new timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd record the full time on twelve difficult repair visits, separating travel, diagnosis and checking on paper. During the first year I'd ask the manager to review the record before reducing paid lead hours, while I kept the repair work. I'd also take any actual proposed wage change to free household advice before Jamie and I made a new spending commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit angry that being good at the difficult work can become a reason to stretch me thinner. I'd still want a practical conversation, not an argument about whether all software is good or bad. I need the hours written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager said your experience should make the shorter visit possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show the actual paid time and ask which task had genuinely disappeared. If there wasn't enough time to do the required checks, I wouldn't accept the shorter promise. Leading the crew includes saying a proposed timetable doesn't fit the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a changed recording procedure became compulsory?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a person to demonstrate a settled required procedure in paid time, with my normal wage and hours maintained. I wouldn't buy a course or start using AI to look agreeable. Until the procedure was clear, I'd keep the approved record method and say what explanation was missing.

say: I'd separate **planning savings** from the travel, fault-finding and checks still needed on site.
I'd request **paper allowances** before promising a shorter visit to customers.
think: My **paid lead hours** could shrink if faster office work encourages the firm to stretch one lead across more crews.
Our **thin reserve** and few alternatives make that risk more than an irritating timetable change.
do: Record **twelve difficult visits** now, separating travel, diagnosis and checking on paper.
Keep repairs and seek a **paid-hours review** before the firm reduces lead coverage.
Check actual wage proposals through **free advice**; require personal instruction on new procedures in paid time with normal wages and hours protected.
feel: **Anxious and frustrated**, seeking written hours and a practical review rather than a broad argument about software.
S1.quote: Leading the crew includes saying a proposed timetable doesn't fit the work.
fieldNote: She identifies **employment pressure** through lead coverage while keeping the job's mostly physical task mix intact.
A required procedure needs **paid personal instruction** with normal wages and hours maintained; this is not voluntary AI learning or funded retraining.

steps.text: Keep leading repairs and record twelve actual difficult visits
Use free advice to check actual proposed wage changes before new spending

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell work thinking systems arrive in 2028 and capable robots reach physical jobs around 2031. My master licence doesn't turn those into the same date or make either harmless. I'd ask for actual paid repair plans rather than a speech about always needing a human face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my paid fitting and repair hours to go once capable robots do that work cheaply. Jamie's physical porter work could change too, so I can't use it as a permanent rescue wage. Three weeks saved is far smaller than the income gap I imagine, and I'd be awake over the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask free household advice to check our mortgage, both wages and essential costs, without assuming any relief would be agreed. In 2029 I'd apply for advertised lead repair roles, leaving only for a signed offer whose pay covered essentials and travel costs. I'd accept changed travel hours only with Jamie agreeing the school pickups, and I'd keep my present paid repairs until all those conditions were met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, though I still know how to make the calls and complete a repair. I'd be frightened of losing a big part of the wage, not ashamed of the skill I have. I can't make our three weeks last until somebody decides what happens after robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no suitable lead vacancy were advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the existing wage and continue checking real adverts, not resign because another firm's website looked busy. There are few electrical employers near us and a signed offer might never come. Advice would help us check the next budget, not create a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about a possible change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'd been asking about work and that we weren't promising a different school or home. Jamie and I would decide the travel and pickup arrangement together before saying yes to anything. My children aren't a transport plan I can rearrange after accepting a job.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking systems** from capable robots reaching physical repairs around 2031.
I'd seek **actual paid work plans**, without treating a master licence or human contact as permanent protection.
think: I expect **large repair-hour losses**, while Jamie's physical wage also lacks a permanent guarantee.
Our **three-week reserve** can't cover the gap I imagine, leaving me awake over the mortgage.
do: Get **free household advice** now using actual mortgage, wage and essential-cost figures, without assuming relief.
Apply for **2029 advertised lead repairs**, leaving only after a signed offer pays essentials and travel.
Accept changed travel hours only with **agreed school pickups**, retaining current work until both conditions are met.
feel: **Alarmed and sleepless**, while retaining practical calls to make and acknowledging that a suitable vacancy may never appear.
S2.quote: My children aren't a transport plan I can rearrange after accepting a job.
fieldNote: Her expected **major income loss** supports alarm despite high skill; neither current seniority nor a nearby website becomes another wage.
The **job-change conditions** preserve an advertised role, signed essential-covering pay after travel, agreed school pickups and current paid work until then.

steps.text: Use free household advice on actual mortgage, wages and essential costs without assuming relief
Apply for advertised lead repairs in 2029; leave only with signed offers covering essentials and travel
Agree changed travel hours and school pickups with Jamie before accepting another job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to check the actual work and a real family timetable before changing anything. Thinking AGI comes in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. I'd still want the firm's paid-hours plan now, not only when the machine order arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hours could shrink, but I don't think a big loss is settled if I can use the warning to find a better arrangement. The mortgage and three-week reserve remain current worries. More time is useful only if I can keep earning while checking the next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the owner for a written account of the next quarter's paid lead hours and bring any shortfall to free household advice. Through the preparation I'd keep the repair job rather than buy an unfamiliar course. In 2032 I'd apply for advertised lead repairs only if I could leave for a signed offer covering essentials and travel costs, with Jamie agreeing changed travel hours and our younger child's school pickup before acceptance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with more room to be careful than in the fast picture. I don't need to make the family timetable fit a job before I know whether the job exists. I'd still want a month in the bank, not just five years on a card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the promised lead hours remained vague?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd point to the dates and ask the owner to explain what was paid work and what was only a possible call. Then I'd take the guaranteed figures home. I wouldn't enter a hopeful conversation as a wage in our household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a better-paid offer made your younger child's school pickup impossible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the present job while looking at another actual vacancy or ask whether a different rota was offered in writing. I wouldn't accept first and leave Jamie to solve our younger child's pickup. A higher rate doesn't pay for an impossible school afternoon.

say: I'd use **five years** to check paid work and the real family timetable before committing.
I'd seek the **lead-hours plan now**, while keeping the thinking and later physical dates distinct.
think: My **hours could shrink**, but checking a workable arrangement gives me control before a large loss is settled.
The **mortgage and thin reserve** still require earnings throughout the preparation years.
do: Request **written quarterly hours** now and use free advice if guaranteed pay leaves a household shortfall.
Keep **paid repairs** rather than buy an unfamiliar course during preparation.
Seek **2032 lead vacancies** with signed pay covering essentials and travel; require Jamie's agreement on changed hours and our younger child's pickup.
feel: **Anxious** with more checking time, without treating a later forecast as a substitute for cash or a workable school afternoon.
S3.quote: A higher rate doesn't pay for an impossible school afternoon.
fieldNote: She retains **present insecurity** despite a longer warning, and distinguishes guaranteed wages from merely possible call-outs.
The **family condition** can block an otherwise better offer; current work remains in place until signed pay and pickup arrangements both work.

steps.text: Keep paid lead repairs and request written quarterly hours
Use free household advice if guaranteed pay leaves an essential-cost shortfall
Apply for advertised lead repairs in 2032; leave only with signed offers covering essentials and travel
Agree changed travel hours and our younger child's school pickup with Jamie before accepting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell friends ten years lets us check a small decision at a time instead of inventing a whole new career today. I'd keep asking the firm for clear paid hours and a person to explain required changes. I don't want the warning to turn every evening at home into a test I'm failing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. The later dates feel less urgent, but low pay and three weeks saved still make ordinary lost shifts worrying now. I can't call the household secure because the machine question is farther away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid repair role now, check guaranteed hours each quarter and use free advice if the basic budget didn't fit. I'd ask for any required procedure to be shown personally within normal paid hours, not promise unpaid study or AI use. In 2037 I'd apply for advertised lead repairs only with a signed offer covering essentials and travel costs, accepting changed travel hours only after Jamie agreed our actual household commitments and keeping current work until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the present money, though not carrying the short robot date into every evening. A decade gives me room to understand a change slowly. It doesn't give the mortgage a slower calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jamie and I would compare actual wages and essential costs, including any changed school needs. If paid hours weakened earlier, we'd bring advice and applications forward. I wouldn't wait for 2036 while a real payslip changed in front of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about your own learning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them I'm good at my work and still ask questions about unfamiliar things. I wouldn't choose their studies from a forecast or count on their future wages. My children's school choices aren't a way for me to repair our household budget.

say: I'd use **ten years** for smaller checked decisions rather than invent a whole new career immediately.
I'd ask for **clear paid hours** and personal explanations of required changes without unpaid household homework.
think: At **53 in 2036**, I'll still need future earnings beyond the later arrival of capable robots.
Our low pay and **thin reserve** keep lost shifts worrying now, despite less urgency about the machine dates.
do: Keep paid repairs and check **guaranteed hours** quarterly, using free advice if essentials don't fit.
Request **personal instruction** for required procedures within normal paid hours, without promising AI use.
Seek **2037 advertised lead work** only with signed essential-covering pay after travel and Jamie agreeing changed hours and actual household commitments.
feel: **Anxious about current bills**, with more room for slow learning and less urgency about robots.
S4.quote: My children's school choices aren't a way for me to repair our household budget.
fieldNote: She remains **resistant to AI** while accepting necessary personal instruction; a master licence doesn't erase the need to ask about unfamiliar systems.
The **later job plan** uses actual household commitments once both children are adults, alongside advertised vacancies, signed pay and travel costs.

steps.text: Keep paid lead repairs and check guaranteed hours quarterly
Use free household advice if guaranteed pay fails to cover essentials
Apply for advertised lead repairs in 2037; leave only with signed offers covering essentials and travel
Agree changed travel hours and actual household commitments with Jamie before accepting another job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect a large part of my repair wage to shrink around 2031 before we have much cash behind us. Written paid hours, free advice using our real budget and personal instruction during paid time would help. I can lead a repair crew without being able to lead the mortgage past a missing wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether a master licence makes it awkward to say money is tight. Sometimes people assume skill, pay and savings are the same thing. I'd like the plan to notice that I have the first without enough of the other two.

headlineQuote: I can lead a repair crew without being able to lead the mortgage past a missing wage.
portrait: At **43**, Sara leads electrical repairs with a two-year technical diploma and master licence, but low pay leaves only three weeks saved.
She and **Jamie**, her hospital-porter partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few nearby electrical employers.
She **never uses AI**, trusts paper fault logs and spoken handovers, and asks for personal paid instruction on required changes.
Her **technical strength** doesn't create cash; fast change alarms her, while longer warnings retain money worries and strict family travel conditions.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before expected large repair-hour losses around 2031, with only a few weeks of reserve.
whatWouldHelp: **Written paid hours**, free advice using actual household figures and personal instruction during paid time would help.
